power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.14", "p = 0.25"), Sentence = c("At a 12-month horizon, the temporal bootstrap indicated improvement (mean ΔWIS = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.18, -0.03]), but the Diebold-Mariano test did not reject equal predictive accuracy (p = 0.14) and bootstrap inference was sensitive to block length (Supplementary Table S3).", "N-BEATS showed the opposite pattern: at one-month forecast horizon there was no consistent advantage for either aggregation strategy across states (median ΔWIS = -0.31; p = 0.25), whereas direct fitting to aggregated case series was favoured from three to 12 month horizons (median ΔWIS = -3.15 to -5.30; Supplementary Table S8)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Accurate and timely probabilistic dengue forecasts can support public health preparedness, but producing reliable forecasts across locations and time horizons remains challenging.

We evaluated five statistical, machine-learning, deep-learning, and foundation-model approaches for forecasting monthly reported dengue cases across 5,570 Brazilian municipalities at 1-, 3-, 6-and 12-month horizons, with forecasts backtested from January 2020 to August 2025.
The time-series foundation model TimesFM maintained comparatively stable probabilistic forecast performance at longer horizons, while most other models showed declining performance.
We then tested whether spatial representations of human and environmental context from a Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) could improve forecasts through post-hoc residual adjustment.

PDFM adjustment improved mean probabilistic forecast performance, measured by the Weighted Interval Score (WIS), in 19 of 20 model-horizon combinations, although the magnitude and frequency of improvements varied across models, horizons and municipalities.

The largest improvements were observed for N-BEATS, including a reduction in mean WIS of 1.13 at the six-month horizon (95% CI [0.84, 1.48]; Diebold-Mariano p < 0.0001), with improvements also observed for XGBoost.
text.formatted: The largest improvements were observed for N-BEATS, including a reduction in mean WIS of 1.13 at the six-month horizon (95% CI [0.84, 1.48]; Diebold-Mariano p < 0.0001), with improvements also observed for XGBoost.

text.text: The proportion of forecasts improved by PDFM generally increased with locally reported dengue case counts, although this relationship varied between models.

Covariate selection, spatial fitting and forecast aggregation strategies showed strong model-dependent effects, while monthly model retraining provided no consistent advantage in the settings evaluated.
Together, these findings highlight the potential of pretrained representations for dengue forecasting, with benefits dependent on forecasting architecture, horizon and modelling configuration.
Dengue is a major vector-borne disease, causing substantial annual morbidity and mortality as well as economic and social disruption.

Dengue virus (DENV) is transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti and, to a lesser degree, Ae. albopictus in tropical and temperate regions, with transmission intensity shaped by climatic, environmental, socioeconomic, demographic and biological factors, including population immunity and circulating DENV serotypes (1).
text.formatted: Dengue virus (DENV) is transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti and, to a lesser degree, Ae. albopictus in tropical and temperate regions, with transmission intensity shaped by climatic, environmental, socioeconomic, demographic and biological factors, including population immunity and circulating DENV serotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(1)</ref>.

text.text: The relative importance of these factors varies over time and by location and is highly context-specific (2).
text.formatted: The relative importance of these factors varies over time and by location and is highly context-specific <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(2)</ref>.

text.text: The number of reported dengue cases reached record levels in 2024, with more than 14 million cases reported worldwide.
In Brazil alone, more than 10 million dengue cases were reported through surveillance notifications, alongside over 6,000 dengue-related deaths (3).
text.formatted: In Brazil alone, more than 10 million dengue cases were reported through surveillance notifications, alongside over 6,000 dengue-related deaths <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(3)</ref>.

text.text: The record epidemic in Brazil and the Americas coincided with El Niño-associated temperature anomalies and substantial southward geographical expansion of dengue transmission into previously less-affected temperate regions (4).
text.formatted: The record epidemic in Brazil and the Americas coincided with El Niño-associated temperature anomalies and substantial southward geographical expansion of dengue transmission into previously less-affected temperate regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(4)</ref>.

text.text: Geographical expansion and increased cases in endemic areas highlight the vulnerability of cities in the Americas to climate-related shifts in temperature and precipitation, creating new challenges for dengue preparedness and response.
Anticipating where and when reported dengue cases will increase, and by how much, is therefore important for targeting preparedness and response.

Probabilistic forecasts characterise uncertainty in these future outcomes rather than providing a single expected trajectory, and can support decisions about where and when public health resources are needed.

Forecasts over longer time horizons, from several months to a year ahead, can inform advance planning and resource allocation across regions, while shorter-term forecasts can support more immediate decisions around healthcare capacity, risk communication and targeted vector-control interventions.

In Brazil, dengue preparedness activities routinely include intensified vector surveillance and campaigns to reduce mosquito breeding sites before seasonal peaks, alongside emergency healthcare mobilisation and redistribution of clinical resources during major epidemics (5) (6) (7).
text.formatted: In Brazil, dengue preparedness activities routinely include intensified vector surveillance and campaigns to reduce mosquito breeding sites before seasonal peaks, alongside emergency healthcare mobilisation and redistribution of clinical resources during major epidemics <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Current approaches to dengue forecasting have primarily relied on historical incidence alongside climatic, demographic and, in some cases, immunological predictors.

Existing approaches include spatiotemporal models incorporating climatic predictors (8) (9) (10), probabilistic models for seasonal epidemic forecasting (11), and ensemble methods combining predictions across multiple models (12) (13) (14).
text.formatted: Existing approaches include spatiotemporal models incorporating climatic predictors <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>, probabilistic models for seasonal epidemic forecasting <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11)</ref>, and ensemble methods combining predictions across multiple models <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(14)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the 2024 edition of the Infodengue-Mosqlimate Dengue Challenge (IMDC24) evaluated probabilistic forecasts from seven statistical and machine-learning models across five Brazilian states, demonstrating substantial variation in performance across models, locations and epidemic seasons, and highlighting the potential value of ensemble approaches (15).
text.formatted: For example, the 2024 edition of the Infodengue-Mosqlimate Dengue Challenge (IMDC24) evaluated probabilistic forecasts from seven statistical and machine-learning models across five Brazilian states, demonstrating substantial variation in performance across models, locations and epidemic seasons, and highlighting the potential value of ensemble approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(15)</ref>.

text.text: However, local population dynamics that shape transmission risk, including human behaviour, mobility, and interactions with the social and built environment, remain difficult to capture fully using conventional epidemiological and climatic covariates (16).
text.formatted: However, local population dynamics that shape transmission risk, including human behaviour, mobility, and interactions with the social and built environment, remain difficult to capture fully using conventional epidemiological and climatic covariates <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16)</ref>.

text.text: The increasing availability of digital data provides new opportunities to characterise these dynamics, including through aggregated signals of mobility, behaviour and population activity.

Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) provides one scalable approach to integrating these heterogeneous factors, learning transferable spatial representations from multimodal information including aggregated search trends, mobility patterns, built-environment characteristics, weather and air quality (17).
text.formatted: Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) provides one scalable approach to integrating these heterogeneous factors, learning transferable spatial representations from multimodal information including aggregated search trends, mobility patterns, built-environment characteristics, weather and air quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(17)</ref>.

text.text: In Brazil, PDFM embeddings have recently shown utility for subnational population estimation, including improvements over traditional hand-crafted geospatial covariates in some settings (18).
text.formatted: In Brazil, PDFM embeddings have recently shown utility for subnational population estimation, including improvements over traditional hand-crafted geospatial covariates in some settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Whether these representations improve predictive performance beyond that achieved by existing infectious disease forecasting models using conventional epidemiological and environmental covariates remains, to our knowledge, unknown.
Beyond representing spatial and contextual information, foundation models can also learn representations of temporal dynamics through large-scale pretraining (19).
text.formatted: Beyond representing spatial and contextual information, foundation models can also learn representations of temporal dynamics through large-scale pretraining <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(19)</ref>.

text.text: Time-series foundation models are trained on large collections of time-series data spanning diverse domains, including those unrelated to infectious diseases, with the aim of learning representations that generalise across downstream forecasting tasks (20, 21).
text.formatted: Time-series foundation models are trained on large collections of time-series data spanning diverse domains, including those unrelated to infectious diseases, with the aim of learning representations that generalise across downstream forecasting tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">21)</ref>.

text.text: Some can be adapted or fine-tuned using taskspecific data to further improve performance (22).

text.text: Recent studies have applied time-series foundation models to infectious-disease forecasting, including dengue and other communicable diseases (12, 23).

text.text: Automated model development using multimodal data and foundation-model embeddings has also shown promise across geospatial prediction tasks, including infectious disease modelling (24).

text.text: Here, we evaluate whether pretrained temporal and spatial representations can strengthen forecasting of dengue epidemic dynamics, measured by monthly reported cases at 1-, 3-, 6-and 12-month horizons.
The analysis encompasses 5,570 municipality-level administrative units across Brazil, including the Federal District and Fernando de Noronha (hereafter collectively referred to as municipalities).

We test two complementary applications of foundation models: a time-series foundation model pretrained on large-scale temporal data, and spatial embeddings from PDFM representing human and environmental characteristics.

We compare five forecasting models spanning statistical, machine-learning, deep-learning and foundation-model paradigms, and assess whether using PDFM embeddings improves probabilistic forecast performance beyond that achieved using historical incidence and conventional covariates.
We further assess how covariate selection, spatial fitting strategy, forecast aggregation and retraining strategy influence forecasting performance.

Finally, we use Empirical Research Assistance (ERA), an Artificial Intelligence (AI) system combining large language models and tree search to iteratively develop scientific software (25), to test whether PDFM embeddings are independently selected for dengue forecasting.

Our findings demonstrate how pretrained temporal and spatial representations can contribute to probabilistic infectious disease forecasting, while highlighting the importance of forecasting architecture and modelling configuration in determining their predictive value.

Across Brazil, the relative performance of the five architectures evaluated depended strongly on forecast horizon, while the benefits of PDFM residual adjustment varied according to the underlying model and epidemiological setting.

These findings extend previous dengue forecasting research demonstrating substantial variation in predictive performance across models, locations and epidemic seasons (12) (13) (14) (15), and suggest that the value of pretrained representations depends not only on the information they encode but also on how that information is incorporated into forecasting systems.

text.text: Whereas most architectures evaluated showed deteriorating probabilistic performance with increasing horizon, TimesFM maintained relatively stable WIS across 3-, 6-and 12-month forecasts.

One possible explanation is that large-scale temporal pretraining enables the model to exploit patterns learned across diverse time series, potentially supporting generalisation beyond the historical dynamics represented in the Brazilian dengue training data.

However, this mechanism cannot be established from the present comparisons, and the observed advantage may also reflect differences in model architecture, probabilistic forecast construction or the configurations evaluated.

TimesFM's performance should therefore be interpreted as evidence for the potential utility of temporal pretraining, rather than demonstrating its superiority over other dengue forecasting approaches.
The potential value of maintaining forecasting performance at seasonal to annual timescales is particularly apparent in the context of dengue's geographical expansion.

The record 2024 epidemics in Brazil and across the Americas, coinciding with El Niño-associated temperature anomalies and expansion into previously less-affected regions (4), highlight the challenges of anticipating changing epidemic dynamics.
Reliable longer-horizon forecasts could support earlier public health preparedness, including advance allocation of resources and planning of vectorcontrol and healthcare responses.
However, their operational value will depend on performance under changing epidemiological conditions and the availability of timely surveillance data.

The model-dependent benefits of PDFM adjustment suggest that pretrained spatial representations can provide predictive information beyond historical dengue cases and conventional covariates, although their utility depends on the forecasting architecture and the errors remaining in its predictions.
PDFM embeddings capture aspects of population activity, connectivity, the built environment and environmental context that may not be fully represented by conventional predictors.
However, larger improvements following adjustment do not necessarily indicate that these representations contain more useful information for a particular model or setting.

Our WIS decomposition showed that improvements arose primarily through reductions in out-of-interval penalties, suggesting that PDFM adjustment may be particularly valuable when baseline predictive distributions fail to capture observed epidemic outcomes.

The geographical analyses further demonstrated that regional differences in absolute WIS improvements were sometimes attenuated when evaluated using log-relative skill, consistent with a contribution from the magnitude and distribution of baseline forecast errors to the apparent heterogeneity.
This interpretation is consistent with the greater improvements observed at higher reported dengue case counts, where forecast errors may also be larger.

Together, these findings suggest that PDFM adjustment benefits depend on the interaction between contextual information, forecasting architecture and residualerror structure, although the specific mechanisms and embedding components responsible remain unresolved.
Geographical variation in baseline forecasting performance was also evident, particularly in southern Brazil.
Although TCN achieved the lowest mean one-month WIS across all five macroregions, its advantage over TimesFM was substantially weaker in Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina than elsewhere.

This raises the possibility that pretrained temporal representations may be comparatively useful where epidemic dynamics differ from historical patterns, although our exploratory analyses of historical dengue activity and changes in reported cases and population-adjusted incidence did not establish a consistent association with relative model performance.

Geographical differences were also apparent in PDFM adjustment benefits, particularly for N-BEATS and XGBoost, suggesting that the contribution of residual adjustment varies across epidemiological settings as well as forecasting architectures.
Together, these findings reinforce the importance of evaluating forecasting approaches across diverse geographical and epidemiological conditions (15).

text.text: The model-dependent effects of covariate selection and spatial fitting suggest that forecasting architecture and modelling configuration should be considered jointly rather than as independent choices.

Additional covariates may improve performance when an architecture can exploit their predictive information, but may provide little benefit or introduce unnecessary complexity when historical epidemic dynamics already capture much of the relevant variation.
Similarly, joint fitting across municipalities may allow models to exploit shared temporal patterns, whereas independent fitting may better preserve locally specific dynamics.

Our results indicate that neither approach is consistently preferable across the architectures evaluated, highlighting the importance of assessing configuration choices within individual forecasting systems rather than assuming that greater model complexity or information sharing necessarily improves performance.
The comparison of state-level forecast aggregation strategies further demonstrates that the preferred approach depends on the forecasting architecture and horizon.
Together, these findings highlight substantial variation in forecasting performance across the models, horizons and modelling configurations evaluated, arguing against a single optimal strategy.

Our comparisons contribute to existing evidence on dengue forecasting in Brazil by informing choices concerning forecasting architecture, horizon, covariate selection, spatial fitting and forecast aggregation (Supplementary Table S12).

text.text: The observed heterogeneity motivates exploring ensemble approaches that combine forecasts from different models or configurations, potentially exploiting complementary strengths across epidemiological settings and forecast horizons.

Evaluating whether such combinations improve predictive performance, and how their contributions should be weighted across locations and horizons, represents an important direction for future research.
The absence of consistent benefits from monthly retraining highlights a potential trade-off between incorporating recent epidemiological information and maintaining stable forecasting performance.

Although frequent updating may allow models to respond to changing epidemic dynamics, it may also introduce variability in fitted parameters without improving predictive accuracy, particularly when recent observations reflect short-term fluctuations rather than persistent changes in transmission.
The numerical instability encountered with N-BEATS further illustrates that computational and implementation considerations can influence the feasibility of frequent model updating.

These findings suggest that retraining frequency should be evaluated as a model-specific design choice, balancing potential improvements in responsiveness against forecast accuracy, computational cost and numerical stability.

However, because our experiments compared only initial training with monthly retraining in Ceará and São Paulo, they do not establish whether alternative updating schedules or adaptation strategies would improve performance.
The ERA experiment provides an independent perspective on the predictive value of PDFM embeddings.

Unlike the primary analyses, which incorporated PDFM through post-hoc residual adjustment, ERA independently selected embedding dimensions to parameterise municipalityspecific characteristics of its forecasting model, including climate sensitivities and forecast uncertainty.

This suggests that PDFM-derived information may contribute to dengue forecasting through modelling approaches beyond residual correction, although neither approach identifies which components of the multimodal representation are responsible for the predictive signal.

The ERA-derived model did not consistently outperform the primary architectures over the hold-out period, but its independent selection of PDFM embeddings provides further support for their contribution to dengue forecasting.
More broadly, our findings illustrate three distinct roles for AI in infectious-disease forecasting.
Time-series foundation models such as TimesFM can transfer representations learned through large-scale temporal pretraining, potentially supporting forecasting across longer horizons.

Geospatial foundation models such as PDFM can provide representations of human and environmental context that augment disease-specific forecasting models, although their benefits depend on the underlying architecture and how these representations are incorporated.
AI-guided model development offers a third approach, identifying and combining predictive information within models developed for a particular task.
These approaches are not necessarily interchangeable, and their relative value will depend on the forecasting objective, available information and modelling framework.

Together, they demonstrate different ways in which AI can contribute to epidemic forecasting, while highlighting the need to evaluate their benefits within specific epidemiological and operational settings.

The variation in forecasting performance across architectures, horizons and modelling configurations highlights the need for flexible, reproducible frameworks that support systematic comparison of forecasting approaches.

The modular Thucia framework (Methods) used in this study was designed to facilitate such comparisons by separating data acquisition, model fitting, probabilistic forecasting, residual adjustment and evaluation into interchangeable components.
This flexibility is particularly relevant when forecasting objectives, data availability and operational requirements differ across geographical settings or change over time.

More broadly, our findings reinforce the importance of benchmarks that evaluate forecasting approaches across different epidemiological contexts, spatial scales and modelling configurations, rather than relying on performance under a single experimental setting.

Such evaluations could help inform model selection and adaptation for operational forecasting, while establishing whether the contextdependent patterns observed in Brazil generalise to other pathogens, geographical settings and surveillance systems.
We acknowledge several limitations.

First, our primary analysis is restricted to Brazil; although this provides a stringent test across diverse epidemiological and climatic settings, generalisability to other countries, pathogens and surveillance systems requires further evaluation.

Second, although we examined correlations among PDFM embedding dimensions and their associations with external spatial characteristics, we did not isolate the contributions of individual embedding components to forecasting performance.

The latent nature of these representations limits mechanistic interpretation, and further component-specific analyses would be needed to establish which behavioural, built-environment or environmental characteristics drive the observed improvements.
Third, the forecasting architectures were selected to represent distinct modelling paradigms rather than to provide an exhaustive benchmark of dengue forecasting methods.

Modelling configurations and hyperparameters were selected pragmatically rather than through exhaustive optimisation, and alternative choices could alter the relative performance of individual models.

Comparisons with additional dengue-specific statistical models and established ensemble approaches would help establish whether the benefits of pretrained representations generalise to other forecasting systems.

The comparison of independent municipality-level and joint stategrouped fitting was also restricted to 20 municipalities with high cumulative reported dengue case counts, limiting the extent to which these configuration-specific findings can be generalised across Brazil.
Direct comparison with recent initiatives such as IMDC24 is further complicated by differences in surveillance outcomes, spatial and temporal resolution, forecast origins and evaluation protocols.

In particular, IMDC24 evaluated weekly forecasts of probable dengue cases at state level over epidemiological seasons, whereas our study evaluates monthly forecasts of notified cases at municipality level across fixed forecast horizons.
A further limitation concerns the potential overlap between TimesFM's pretraining data and the data used in this study.

Although TimesFM was applied without task-specific parameter fine-tuning, potential overlap between the study data and its pretraining corpus cannot be completely ruled out because the composition of the pretraining data is not exhaustively identifiable at the individual-series level.
Fourth, the retraining analysis was restricted to monthly updating in Ceará and São Paulo, and a valid comparison could not be made for N-BEATS because of numerical instability.
Finally, all primary analyses were retrospective and depended on the quality and completeness of the underlying surveillance data.

Historical reporting vintages were not reconstructed, and forecasts were generated and evaluated using a frozen retrospective InfoDengue extraction in which historical case counts may incorporate revisions made after the corresponding forecast origin.

The evaluation also encompassed the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent large dengue epidemics, during which epidemiological and surveillance changes may have affected relationships learned from historical data.
Furthermore, historical PDFM embeddings aligned to individual forecast origins were unavailable, and a single October 2023 snapshot was used throughout the evaluation period.
These limitations mean that the findings should be interpreted as retrospective evidence rather than established operational forecasting performance.
In conclusion, our findings demonstrate the potential of pretrained temporal and spatial representations to strengthen probabilistic dengue forecasting in Brazil.

Among the five architectures evaluated, TimesFM maintained stronger relative performance at longer forecast horizons, while PDFM-derived spatial representations provided additional predictive information for several models through residual adjustment.
However, these benefits depended on forecasting architecture, horizon and geographical setting, with modelling configuration further influencing predictive performance.

Together, these findings highlight the importance of evaluating forecasting approaches across different epidemiological and operational contexts, rather than assuming that any single architecture or configuration will perform consistently best.

Integrating pretrained representations into dengue forecasting systems therefore offers opportunities to improve predictive performance, but their practical value will require further validation under operational forecasting conditions.

text.text: Second, for the 20 municipalities with the highest cumulative reported dengue case counts over the study period, we compared municipality-level forecasts from models fitted independently to each municipality with forecasts for the same municipalities from models fitted jointly across municipalities within each state.

Third, we compared two approaches to generating state-level forecasts across all 27 Brazilian states: fitting models directly to state-level aggregated case series and aggregating municipality-level probabilistic forecasts after model fitting.

For the state-level forecast-aggregation analysis, municipality-level predictive distributions were combined using Monte Carlo simulation because quantiles of municipality-level forecasts cannot be directly summed to obtain quantiles of the state-level predictive distribution.
For each municipality, a predictive distribution was approximated by interpolation between forecast quantiles.

Joint draws from municipality-level distributions were generated using a Gaussian copula with a fixed dependence parameter of ρ = 0.3, selected pragmatically to represent moderate positive dependence between municipality-level forecasts without assuming either independence or strong spatial dependence.
Simulated municipality-level case counts were summed within each state, and quantiles of the resulting simulated state-level distribution were used as the aggregated probabilistic forecast.
Observed state-level case counts were obtained by summing reported municipality-level cases.
For each of the three modelling-configuration comparisons, forecasts were paired by spatial unit, target month and forecast horizon.
Differences in WIS were calculated between paired configurations and averaged across the January 2020-August 2025 target-month evaluation period within each spatial unit.
The resulting municipality-or state-level mean differences were summarised by their mean, median and interquartile range.
Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were applied to the paired spatial-unit summaries where inferential comparisons were reported.
Thus, the inferential unit for these analyses was the municipality or state after averaging forecastperformance differences through time.
As a separate secondary analysis, we evaluated monthly iterative retraining in municipality-level experiments in Ceará and São Paulo.
Under the initial training regime, each model was fitted once using data from January 2010 to December 2019 and was not subsequently retrained during the evaluation period.

Under monthly retraining, models were refitted at each monthly forecast interval using an expanding training window, retaining the original January 2010 start date and incorporating all observations available up to the corresponding forecast origin.

WIS was averaged across the January 2020-August 2025 target-month evaluation period within each municipality, and paired municipality-level means were compared using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
Retraining comparisons were reported only for model-state combinations for which usable paired forecasts were available; numerical failures were recorded separately.
TimesFM was excluded because its pretrained model parameters were not fitted or fine-tuned to the study data, making iterative retraining inapplicable.
Models were evaluated primarily using the Weighted Interval Score (WIS), a proper scoring rule for probabilistic forecasts (40) that assesses predictive calibration and sharpness.
WIS was calculated on the log(1 + cases) scale to reduce the influence of differences in absolute reported case counts across municipalities and time.
Lower WIS values indicate better probabilistic forecast performance.
The coefficient of determination (R²) was used as a complementary measure of agreement between point predictions and observed reported case counts.

For the analysis in Figure 2C, we constructed a seasonal reference forecast separately for each municipality and calendar month using only observations from the January 2010-December 2019 training period.
text.formatted: For the analysis in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2C</ref>, we constructed a seasonal reference forecast separately for each municipality and calendar month using only observations from the January 2010-December 2019 training period.

text.text: For each municipality-calendar-month combination, the seasonal reference forecast was defined as the mean log(1 + cases) across the corresponding calendar month in the training years.

This value was used for all predictive quantiles, yielding a degenerate predictive distribution centred on the historical seasonal mean, and was held fixed throughout the January 2020-August 2025 evaluation period.
The baseline was scored using the same quantile grid and WIS implementation as the forecasting models.

For each matched municipality and target month, model skill relative to the seasonal baseline was calculated as log(1 + WISseasonal) -log(1 + WISmodel), such that positive values indicate lower WIS, and therefore better probabilistic forecast performance, for the forecasting model.

To characterise how PDFM adjustment affected probabilistic forecast performance, we separated the constituent WIS terms (40) into contributions from median forecast error, predictive-interval width and out-of-interval penalties.

For each paired PDFM-adjusted and base forecast, the change in each component was calculated as the PDFM-adjusted contribution minus the corresponding base-forecast contribution, such that negative values indicate an improvement.
Component-wise differences were then averaged across municipality-month forecasts; their sum equals the total mean ΔWIS.

To examine whether the effect of PDFM adjustment varied with observed dengue case counts, municipality-month forecasts were stratified retrospectively according to the number of reported cases in the forecast target month.
Observations with zero reported cases formed a separate stratum.

Within each target month and model-horizon combination, observations with positive reported case counts were divided into low, moderate and high strata using the 33rd and 67th percentiles of their case-count distribution.
For each stratum, we calculated the proportion of paired forecasts for which PDFM adjustment reduced WIS (ΔWIS < 0).
text.formatted: For each stratum, we calculated the proportion of paired forecasts for which PDFM adjustment reduced WIS (ΔWIS < 0).

text.text: To quantify the magnitude of these effects, mean ΔWIS was calculated within each stratum and target month, then averaged equally across target months.
High-minus-low contrasts were calculated as paired differences between monthly mean ΔWIS values in the highest and lowest positive case-count strata.
Uncertainty was estimated using a temporal moving-block bootstrap with three-month blocks and 2,000 replicates, with sensitivity analyses using six-and twelve-month blocks.
These stratified analyses were exploratory, and confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
For comparisons involving PDFM residual adjustment, mean differences in WIS were evaluated using a temporal moving-block bootstrap (41) to account for chronological dependence.
text.formatted: For comparisons involving PDFM residual adjustment, mean differences in WIS were evaluated using a temporal moving-block bootstrap <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(41)</ref> to account for chronological dependence.

text.text: For each model and forecast horizon, ΔWIS was first averaged across municipalities within each target month to form a chronological sequence, from which contiguous blocks of three months were resampled with replacement.
The 95% confidence interval was defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 2,000 bootstrap replicates.
Sensitivity analyses used block lengths of 6 and 12 months.

As a complementary test of predictive accuracy, we applied two-sided Diebold-Mariano tests (42, 43) to chronological target-month sequences of mean WIS, obtained by averaging WIS across municipalities within each target month.
text.formatted: As a complementary test of predictive accuracy, we applied two-sided Diebold-Mariano tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">43)</ref> to chronological target-month sequences of mean WIS, obtained by averaging WIS across municipalities within each target month.

text.text: The dependence parameter was set to the forecast horizon, with a Bartlett variance estimator and Harvey small-sample correction.
To account for multiple testing across the 20 model-horizon comparisons, statistical significance was assessed using a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of α = 0.0025 (0.05/20).
SARIMA produced occasional extreme predictions in a small number of municipalities, particularly at longer forecast horizons.

Across the evaluation period, the forecast median exceeded one million cases in 13 of 1,515,584 municipality-month-horizon forecasts (<0.001%): none at the 1-month horizon, one at 3 months, three at 6 months, and nine at 12 months.
text.formatted: Across the evaluation period, the forecast median exceeded one million cases in 13 of 1,515,584 municipality-month-horizon forecasts (<0.001%): none at the 1-month horizon, one at 3 months, three at 6 months, and nine at 12 months.

text.text: These finite extreme forecasts were retained in the quantitative WIS evaluation to avoid artificially improving estimated forecast performance, but were excluded from selected visualisations where their magnitude would otherwise obscure the displayed forecast trajectories.
As a complementary analysis, we used Google's Empirical Research Assistance (ERA) to develop a probabilistic dengue forecasting model across all Brazilian municipalities.

ERA was provided with historical reported dengue case counts, climatic and ecological covariates, municipality-level spatial adjacency and static PDFM embeddings, and was tasked with minimising mean Weighted Interval Score (WIS) across 1-, 3-, 6-and 12-month forecast horizons.

Model development preserved temporal ordering of the epidemiological observations, such that forecasts at each origin used only observations assigned to that date or earlier; the static PDFM embeddings were fixed across forecast origins as described above.
Model development and optimisation used target observations through August 2023.
The resulting forecasting function was then frozen and evaluated against the September 2023-August 2025 hold-out period, which was not used during model development or optimisation.
The final ERA-derived model used municipality-and month-specific historical reported case counts to define seasonal baselines, adjusted according to recent deviations from local seasonal patterns.
Recent epidemic momentum was partially propagated between neighbouring municipalities through the spatial adjacency network and progressively damped with increasing forecast horizon.
Climatic information was incorporated through the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) and six-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-6).
Selected dimensions of the static PDFM embeddings parameterised municipality-specific climate sensitivities, baseline dispersion and forecast volatility (Supplementary Table S11).
